strengths: SGDRO addresses a relevant problem for visual recognition: maintaining minority-group accuracy under distribution shift. Its combination of an aggregate-loss SAM perturbation with Group-DRO updates is simple and potentially useful when group annotations are available. Algorithm 1 makes the main procedure understandable.

The controlled comparison against GDRO on Waterbirds provides positive evidence. With the same strong regularization, SGDRO improves worst-group accuracy from 86.5% to 87.2%, group-average accuracy from 90.4% to 90.6%, and both minority groups' accuracies (Table 1). Experiments use five random seeds.

Evaluation covers six DomainBed datasets with three seeds and training-domain validation for model selection. SGDRO achieves 71.4% average accuracy, compared with 70.9% for ERM and 70.1% for GDRO (Table 3), supporting some usefulness beyond Waterbirds.

The curvature analysis complements the accuracy results. Under matched regularization, SGDRO reduces both reported leading Hessian eigenvalues relative to GDRO in every Waterbirds group (Table 2), providing empirical support for its flatness motivation.
weaknesses: The principal technical concern is that the claimed guarantees of shared flat minima and worst-group generalization are not established. The Taylor expansion in Section 3.1 uses overall-loss derivatives throughout, whereas expanding Equation 3 requires the worst-group gradient and Hessian, with the overall-loss gradient supplying the perturbation direction. Correcting this notation would still leave no generalization or flatness guarantee: a perturbation chosen to increase average loss need not expose a particular group's sharp directions. The empirical curvature measurements support an observation, not the stated guarantees.

The contribution's distinguishing choices are insufficiently isolated. There is no comparison with SAM applied directly to the Group-DRO loss, no ablation of aggregate-loss versus group-loss perturbations, and no SAM baseline in DomainBed. Consequently, the results do not establish why this particular coupling improves on a straightforward combination of the existing methods. Additionally, Waterbirds comparisons against ERM/SAM change the regularization coefficient from 0.0001 to 1.0, confounding attribution of the larger robustness and curvature differences; the matched GDRO comparison remains informative.

The evidence does not support the claimed reduction in the average-versus-worst-group trade-off. In Table 1, the 0.7-point worst-group improvement over GDRO accompanies a decrease in weighted average accuracy from 93.8% to 93.1%, with both majority groups declining. The gain is also modest relative to the reported per-group variability, and uncertainty for the improvement itself is not provided. DomainBed reports average target-domain accuracy, so it supplies limited additional evidence specifically about worst-group performance.

Reproducibility is only partial. References to the GDRO and DomainBed protocols help, but the manuscript does not specify the DomainBed perturbation-radius search space, explicit backbone and training configurations, or detailed minibatch handling of groups. Table 1 also leaves the meaning of its error bars unspecified. These reporting issues are secondary to the unsupported central guarantees and missing comparisons needed to establish the value of the proposed coupling, which determine my weak-reject recommendation.
